events.title: Hands in the Soil, Legs on the Pole: Queerness in the Material Realm
events.blurb:
FREE, $10-$15 suggested donation

Sponsored by Yerba Buena Gardens Festival & Yerba Buena Partnership
Media sponsorship by 48 Hills
A part of the Litquake Out Loud series

How is a tree like a stripper pole? Where do the poetics of physicality and ecology overlap? As digital spaces collapse into slop and surveillance, how can queer communities in the material world dig and twerk toward pleasure and liberation? Here, QTBIPOC writers Brandon Logans, Kevin Madrigal Galindo, May-Li Khoe, and Nnenna Loveth explore the sensuality, tenderness, and resilience of both body and earth. These landworkers, dancers, and poets discuss how queerness informs and supports their relationship to tangible space, natural environs, and embodied movement. Curated by Mukethe Kawinzi.

events.title: Fluent in Rebirth: Trans and Non-Binary Incantations
events.blurb:
FREE, $10-$15 suggested donation
 
Sponsored by Yerba Buena Gardens Festival & Yerba Buena Partnership
 Media sponsorship by 48 Hills
 A part of the Litquake Out Loud series
 
If you’re looking for architects to dream up a new world, why not start with the folks who have already built one? As trans and gender non-confirming people, we are skilled at identifying what is meant to stifle and cage us, as well as envisioning what else is possible when we rage towards liberation. Trans people teach us what it means to transform the physical conditions of our world and show us what’s possible when our imaginations are freest and at their most feral. These Bay Area trans and non-binary artists will share work resisting erasure and conjuring prayers for the world we’re collectively building. Featuring Isa Borgeson, Mason J, Trinh Lê, and Reggie Edmonds-Vazquez. Curated by Zara Jamshed.

events.title: Queer Trans Black & Indigenous Poetics: We Have Always Paved Our Own Ways
events.blurb:
FREE, $10-$15 suggested donation
 
Sponsored by Yerba Buena Gardens Festival & Yerba Buena Partnership
 Media sponsorship by 48 Hills
 A part of the Litquake Out Loud series
 
Queer trans Black and Indigenous people have always paved our own ways of existing in the world, formed our own networks of care, and resisted dominant systems of power to preserve culture, traditions, and our ways of life. This reading will gather queer and trans Black and Indigenous poets Aleah Bradshaw, Ju(mia), and Zander Moreno Lozano to explore relation to the body, land, lineage, resistance, and the alternative futures we are actively building. Please join us for an afternoon of shared joy, righteous wordsmithing, and compelling truth. Curated by Vania Luna Gutierrez.

events.title: An Evening with Ayad Akhtar
events.blurb:
$53 with code LITQUAKE5
 
Co-presented with City Arts & Lectures
 
A mysterious accident along a country road sparks an awakening and an investigation in Pulitzer Prize–winning playwright and acclaimed novelist Ayad Akhtar’s most daring work yet—a visionary novel of spiritual transformation in an age of fracture—"bordering at times on the ineffable" (Mary Gaitskill).
 
When a hit-and-run shatters more than his body, a writer is caught between revelation and madness as an uncanny pull toward a brilliant campus colleague ensnares him in a scandal that threatens to destroy them both. What begins as a provocative portrait of academic and cultural warfare deepens into erotic entanglement, the exposure of a family secret, and the mystery surrounding the narrator’s accident—both the violence and its aftermath. In conversation with Karen Russell. Doors at 7:00pm.

events.title: Kidquake: Upper Elementary
Litquake's Opening Night Bash: Booksellers Ball
events.blurb:
$50 / $75 to sponsor a bookseller or librarian
All sales help support the rest of Litquake's (75% free!) festival programming!

Co-presented with Book Passage, Black Bird Books, Bookshop West Portal, City Lights, Dog Eared Books, East Bay Booksellers, Et al., Fabulosa Books, Green Apple Books, Noe Valley Books, Pegasus Books, Sistah Scifi, Telegraph Hill Books, The Booksmith, The Love Potion Library, Medicine for Nightmares, and Womb House Books

Beverages sponsored by Griffo Distillery, Lagunitas Brewing Company, & Saintsbury Winery

Kick off the 2026 festival at the Booksellers Ball, our big opening night bash! Here, the Litquake community will come together to fête San Francisco’s independent bookstores at the former home of the legendary Paper Doll, an underground LGBTQ supper club active 1941-1969.

Join us for catered event with abundant libations and a special literature-themed drag performance from Carlota Di Carlo. With festive grooves from BFF.FM DJ Lead Teddy and an open bar from beverage sponsors Griffo Distillery and Saintsbury Winery, we invite you to kick up your heels with local literati and celebrate another year of Litquake!

events.title: Kidquake: Lower Elementary
events.blurb:
FREE
 

 Book donations sponsored by Candlewick Press
 Co-presented with San Francisco Public Library
 

 Our acclaimed Kidquake programs for children’s books; authors, illustrators, poets, and bookmakers provide readings, discussions, and workshops designed to fuel kids’ imagination. This morning’s two sessions, for kids in 1st and 2nd grades, begin at 10:15am and 11:15am. Featuring authors Mahogany L. Browne and Maggie Tokuda-Hall plus an activity led by the Randall Museum of Science, with workshops (by lottery) from author/illustrator of Ren’s Pencil Bo Lu (illustration) and author of A Year of Kites Monisha Bajaj (kite-making). Advance sign-up required for in-person student groups. Streamed live at youtube.com/SanFranciscoLibrary.

events.title: An Afternoon with Mahogany Browne
events.blurb:
FREE

Co-presented with Chapter 510

Calling all teens, educators, and families! Take a breather after the busy school week at Chapter 510’s cozy space for creative writing. As part of their Write, Speak, Heal collaborative with Youth Speaks and Divine Radiance, join poet, playwright, organizer, and educator Mahogany L. Browne for an afternoon celebrating young people’s self-expression, resilience, and wellness. Browne will read from her National Book Award–longlisted collection of stories and poems A Bird in the Air Means We Can Still Breathe, which Publishers Weekly calls a “love letter to [a] resilient teen population as they adjust to a changed world.” Joining her will be Chapter 510 teaching artist Belinda Bellinger, with an opening performance by Youth Speaks poets. Followed by a conversation around creativity, healing, and resilience moderated by Alie Jones. Doors at 4pm.

events.title: "I took the lake between my legs": Women of a Certain Age Read Poems on Sex and Death
events.blurb:
$12 adv / $15 door

Co-presented with Left Margin Lit and Vintage Berkeley

Back by popular demand, with an all-new lineup! Sex and death are central human concerns, but older women poets often find themselves silenced or sidelined on the first of these subjects. Here, in an event curated by Rebecca Foust, five women aged 40 and better—Mahogany L. Browne, Prageeta Sharma, Jen Siraganian, Melissa Stein, and Barbara Jane Reyes—will share frankly erotic work that refuses to be muted or mooted and makes a bulwark of bodily sensuality against death, time, and our aging selves. Alongside the reading, emceed by poet Tracey Knapp, winemaker Emily Fernwood will be on site to introduce Osa Major wines, which will be available for purchase by the glass. This event will take place on Vintage Berkeley’s secret garden patio—dress accordingly! Doors at 5:30pm.

events.title: Olivie Blake: Dreamland
events.blurb:
Pay-what-you-can for guaranteed seat; FREE to walk-ups (space depending)

Get in the spirit of scary season with the latest moody masterpiece from bestselling novelist Olivie Blake, author of Girl Dinner. Loosely inspired by the 1947 Black Dahlia murder, Dreamland is a dark Hollywood fable about fame, ambition, and the price some people are willing to pay to achieve both. Alix E. Harrow calls it nothing short of a “gory, gothic masterpiece.” In conversation with Kristina Ten, whose work Blake selected for the latest Best American Science Fiction and Fantasy anthology. Dress in your Hollywood finery (or come as you are) and bring your burning questions for Olivie Blake! Doors at 6:30pm.

events.title: Hernan Diaz: Ply
events.blurb:
$15 gen admission / $40 with signed book
 
Centuries from now, at the dawn of a historical epoch filled with both uncertainty and promise, an orphan is adrift in a city on the brink of a great transformation...After rewriting America’s past with his two previous novels, Pulitzer Prize winner Hernan Diaz defies expectations with his third and turns to the future with a novel that examines the place of technology in the American imagination. Combining Dickensian odyssey, family drama, and scientific thriller, Ply poignantly charts the tenuous boundaries of selfhood and the distance that inevitably stands between us and those we love. In conversation with Pulitzer Prize–winning science writer and friend Ed Yong. Doors at 6:30pm.

events.title: From Punchlines to Gut Punches: Weaponizing Wit With Humor and Satire
Beyond the Isms: Crafting Stories that Spark Real-World Activism
Lick, Smack, Slurp: Writing the Desires We Only Confess to the Page
¡Poetry on la Veinticuatro! Poets in the Window
events.blurb:
FREE, $10-$15 suggested donation
 
A reading series that puts poets in the front window of the bookstore to read their poems to the chingadera, locura, and beauty that is 24th Street. Featuring Mukethe Kawinzi, hector son of hector, Barbara Jane Reyes, and San Francisco’s current Poet Laureate Genny Lim.

events.title: Literary Speakeasy Presents: Dragging Celebrity Autobiographies
¡Poetry on la Veinticuatro! Pan Dulce Poets
events.blurb:
FREE, $10-$15 suggested donation
 
We will make our way down 24th, to a 49-year-old Mission institution, La Reyna Bakery, for the Pan Dulce Poets, a beloved Mission series started in May of 2015 by Ricardo Tavarez. Here, poets read surrounded by pan dulce and used a converted paleta cart as a podium while Louie passed out cafecito y chocolate caliente to everyone. Featuring Ellie Lopez, Pan Dulce Poets founder Ricardo Tavarez, Michelle Ibarra, and former San Francisco Poet Laureate Alejandro Murguía.

events.title: Min Jin Lee: American Hagwon (SOLD OUT)
Claudia Rankine: Triage
events.blurb:
Pay-what-you-can for guaranteed seating; FREE to walk-ups (space depending)

Sponsored by Alta Journal
Co-presented with First Presbyterian Church of Oakland

Poet Claudia Rankine’s work is unfailingly expansive—broadening readers’ understanding of race, social conscience, and the limits of genre. Triage, Rankine’s first book since the groundbreaking “American” trilogy (whose centerpiece, Citizen, was a 2023 Alta California Book Club selection), again defies boundaries. Here Rankine traces a decades-long friendship between two women—the narrator and the theorist—following their evolving relationship against a backdrop of ever-more-turbulent times. Here Rankine creates a politically urgent, uncategorizable mix of essay, criticism, memoir, and photography that Booklist calls “Startlingly original ... A remarkable, soul-stirring work.” In conversation with Cathy Park Hong, whose award-winning nonfiction book Minor Feelings engages intimately with Rankine’s ideas. The Alta Journal team will be on hand to introduce you to upcoming California Book Club selections, and we’ll kick things off with performances by 2026 Oakland Youth Poet Laureate Isaiah Kahn, Vice OYPL Isabel Shen, and OYPL finalist Lina Norris-Raman. Doors at 6:30pm.

events.title: Poetry World Series: Litquake Edition
events.blurb:
$15 adv / $20 door
21+

Two teams of award-winning poets, including Bhion Achimba, Rhoni Blankenhorn, Safia Elhillo, Prageeta Sharma, Angel Dominguez, and Ben Gucciardi, take turns batting at topics pitched to them by the audience. Fastballs, curveballs, knuckleballs: these poets won’t know what’s coming next! Hilarity and brilliance both guaranteed. Daniel Handler will be tonight’s emcee, and eminently qualified umpires—Randall Mann and Katie Peterson—will score each batter’s reading. The winning team takes the series title. Don’t forget to bring a topic to stump the poets with! Book sales/signing follow the final inning. Doors at 6:30pm.

events.title: ¡Poetry on la Veinticuatro! La Lunada
events.blurb:
FREE, $10-$15 suggested donation
 
 Finally we will end the crawl at the mama of all Mission reading series, La Lunada! Originally started in 1998 in a Mexican restaurant in San Jose, La Lunada relocated to Calle 24 in 2004 at the original location of Galeria de la Raza on the esquina of 24th and Bryant. Since then the Lunada has been where countless poets from the neighborhood and beyond have gathered and celebrated the power of poesía. Featuring Kevin Madrigal Galindo, Rebeca Abidaíl Flores, and Know Expressions.

events.title: Voice Lessons: Crafting an Artist Statement that Proves You're Human
events.blurb:
Pay-what-you-can for guaranteed seat; FREE to walk-ups (space depending)

Sponsored by Yerba Buena Partnership

If you’re trying to land grants, residencies, or funding, how can you write a compelling artist statement without hiding behind generic grant-speak, clinical jargon, or AI buzzwords? Author Janine Kovac will lead book critic Britta Stromeyer, publicist Cristina Deptula, and literary agent Rachel Neumann in a discussion on tapping into the genuine voice that allows an author to speak about their own work with clarity and authenticity. Learn tips and tricks for elevating your artistic narrative while keeping your unique point-of-view front and center!

events.title: The Unconventional Author: Side Doors and Secret Passages to Publication
The Savage Mind: An American Legacy with David Treuer
events.blurb:
FREE, $10-$15 suggested donation
 
Co-presented with Grace Cathedral’s The Forum
 
“Unlike anything I have read…this book will make a mark.” —Percival Everett, Pulitzer Prize– and National Book Award–winning author. In the wake of George Floyd’s murder and the January 6 insurrection, as America seemed to be falling apart, New York Times bestseller and National Book Award finalist David Treuer decided to hold himself and his family together the only way he knew how: he sat down to write a letter. Ranging from Treuer’s upbringing on the Leech Lake reservation in Minnesota to the experiences of his parents, a Jewish Holocaust refugee and the first American Indigenous woman judge, The Savage Mind reveals the terrifying essence of our nation: frontier violence, which has defined our country, our culture, and our very selves. In conversation with Grace Cathedral’s The Very Rev. Malcolm Clemens Young. The Forum is a series of stimulating conversations about faith and ethics in relation to the important issues of our day. Doors at 12:30pm.

events.title: Lesbians Are Elsewhere: Writing the For All Gaze Archive
events.blurb:
FREE, $10-$15 suggested donation
 
This summer, lesbian and queer writers of the Bay wrote in response to the Oakland-based F.A.G. Archive (For All Gaze Archive), a personal collection of queer publications and flyers from 1970–2000s created and run by Sasha Fuentes. Hear our writers perform their responses and hang around to peruse select publications from the archive pulled for this special viewing. Featuring Elena Gross, Sloane Holzer, and curator Jaelynn Walls. Doors at 1:30pm.

events.title: After The Launch: Raising Your Book to Survive and Thrive
Natalie Baszile: Friends and Family
Out on the Table: Writers on Food with Garrett Schlichte
events.blurb:
Pay-what-you-can for guaranteed seat; FREE to walk-ups (space depending)
 
Sponsored by Gazetteer SF
 Co-presented with Kitchen Table Reading Series
 
Celebrating the upcoming release of Garrett Schlichte's debut collection of essays, Dinner Party Stories, the Kitchen Table reading series and curator Micheal Foulk bring Schlichte together with chef Gaby Maeda and writer Jennifer Barone to discuss food, writing, identity, and the secrets to living life as deliciously as possible. Hosted at Stephen Wade's delectable SOMA eatery, The Nosh Box. Doors at 7:00pm.

events.title: Invitation | Abandonment: A Collective Poem in Assembly
events.blurb:
FREE, $10–15 suggested donation
 
Rooted in practices of care, vulnerability, and experimentation, this event asks: how do we dwell in the spaces between spaces? And what must we invite or abandon there to return more connected, understanding, and whole? Featuring readings from poets aracelis girmay, Ladan Khoddam-Khorasani, Gabriel Cortez, and Dora Prieto. Come listen, come help write a collaborative closing poem drawn from the room. Doors at 5:30pm.

events.title: Tilar J. Mazzeo: The Sea Captain’s Wife
events.blurb:
$5 MI members / $15 gen public
 
Co-presented with Mechanics' Institute

 New York Times bestseller Tilar J. Mazzeo brings us The Sea Captain's Wife, the true story of the first female captain of a merchant ship and her treacherous navigation of Antarctica's deadly waters. In 1856, at just nineteen years old, Mary Ann Patten led her crew through Drake's Passage as her husband, the former captain, lay deathly ill and the first mate agitated for mutiny. Set against the backdrop of the California Gold Rush and taking us to the brink of Antarctica, The Sea Captain's Wife draws on new archival research from nineteenth-century women’s maritime journals and on Mazzeo’s own expedition to the Southern Ocean and Antarctica in search of Mary Ann’s route. Doors at 6:00pm.

events.title: NBCC Presents: The Author/Critic Dilemma
events.blurb:
FREE, $10–15 suggested donation

Media sponsorship by Publishers Weekly
Co-presented with National Book Critics Circle & Cita Press

Writers who wear multiple hats, as Virginia Woolf did, will share what they’ve learned from the writer and literary critic extraordinaire as authors/poets/critics today. Their wide-ranging conversation will touch on everything from ethical considerations to the vulnerabilities of being deep in the creative writing process when your strong critical voice rears its ugly head. With May-lee Chai, Jane Ciabattari, Jonathan Leal, Greg Sarris, and moderator Iris Jamahl Dunkle, as well as special guest Jessi Haley, editor of Cita Press, publisher of Luminous Halo: Selected Writings by Virginia Woolf. Doors at 6:30pm.

events.title: Asale Angel-Ajani: Fugitive Archives Launch
events.blurb:
FREE, $10–15 suggested donation

Co-presented with Pegasus Books
Asale Angel-Ajani will discuss Fugitive Archives: An American Family and the Myth of Belonging—an incisive, lyrical exploration of one family's history that radically overturns American myths about race, violence, and belonging. In conversation with Carvell Wallace, who has called Fugitive Archives “courageous, impressive, and deeply powerful.”

events.title: Which Side? A Protest Music Teach-Out
events.blurb:
$30 advance/$35 at door

Co-presented with KQED Live and Amoeba Music

Every movement has a soundtrack. Hear how protest songs become anthems that inspire resistance, build solidarity, and propel social change with a special San Francisco edition of Which Side?: A Protest Music Teach-Out. Acclaimed artists Diana Gameros, The Sam Chase, and Marcus Shelby join host James Sullivan to perform and unpack classic and original protest songs and celebrate the Bay Area's rich tradition of resistance, activism, and galvanizing music. Doors at 6:00pm.

events.title: While you were novel-ing, I studied the blade: A Celebration of the Short Story
Writing The Body: Sports and Identity
events.blurb:
FREE, $10-15 suggested donation

Iron Man triathlete Swetha Amit and outdoor adventure sports veteran Yi Shun Lai–both writers as well as athletes– dig deep into the process of writing about identities and bodies shaped by their dedication to sport. Who are you, when you can no longer compete, or when competing is no longer enough? Are some extremes irrecoverable once they’ve been reached? How might one heal, or insist on being more than just a winner? What does it mean to compete in white and male-dominated sports as Asian American athletes, and how do issues of race and gender play into dominant cultural narratives around individual athletic achievement? In conversation with author and former pro-wrestler Michael Copperman. Doors at 6:00pm.

events.title: Passages of Babel: Translation and the Book Arts of Servane Briand
events.blurb:
FREE, $10-$15 suggested donation

Part of Words Around the World
Sponsored by Center for the Art of Translation
Co-presented with San Francisco Center for the Book

Center for the Art of Translation and San Francisco Center for the Book join Litquake to present an evening showcasing the sculptural artists' books of Bay Area artist Servane Briand. The event centers on Passages of Babel, her investigation into language and translation, and what is lost or invented in the act of moving meaning from one tongue to another. All three books in the series will be on view: Arise by Any Other Name, A Comme Babel, and Making Sense, each made in collaboration with poets and translators.

The evening will feature a reading by Servane Briand and her collaborators, Patrick Fenton and Samuel Mignot. Following the reading, Olivia Sears will lead a conversation with Patrick, Samuel and Servane to reflect on translation understood not as a shift between two languages but as a collaborative, multi-dimensional process bridging text, physical structure, and design. Whether you are an avid reader of translated literature, a contemporary art lover, or a design enthusiast, this evening offers a rare chance to engage with books as living, multidimensional sculptures and to experience translation as a physical, tactile journey. Doors at 6:00pm.

events.title: West Coast Beat: The SF Roots of Rolling Stone
events.blurb:
$15 (includes museum admission)

Sponsored by Reed Schmidt
Co-presented with Counterculture Museum

Today’s shiny exteriors and inscrutable billboards can’t entirely obliterate San Francisco’s defining role in literature, activism, visual arts, and, yes, music. That storied history includes the 1967 founding of Rolling Stone. As both Peter Richardson and Charles Ponce de Leon relate in recent books, for a decade (before decamping for NYC), the magazine was at the vanguard of West Coast counterculture, launching dozens of journalists’ careers and setting new standards for writing about music and culture. Where better, then, to reunite folks with first-hand knowledge of those SF roots, including Ben Fong-Torres and Marianne Partridge, than at the new Counterculture Museum? Music journalist James Sullivan will take us back in time, as together we compile a scrapbook of the music, writing, and memories that defined the magazine—and the moment. Doors at 6:30pm.

events.title: Trading Pages: A Poetry/Fiction Exchange
events.blurb:
$12 adv / $15 door
 
Yin and yang? Or oil and water? Join us for this special, hopefully amicable exchange between fiction writers and poets…and no, they are not the unwitting subjects of an elaborate bet. This summer, Zach Williams traded pages with Judy Halebsky, Vanessa Hua with Dean Rader, and Kate Folk with Cintia Santana. Join us as these writers come together to read and respond in appreciation and celebration of each other’s narrative arcs and line breaks. Moderated by Litquake Artistic Director Graham Todd. Doors at 6:30pm.

events.title: Jon Ronson: Adventures in a World of Unraveling Men
events.blurb:
$20 gen admission / $42 with book
 
Media sponsorship by 48 Hills
Co-presented with JCCSF
 
From the bestselling author of The Psychopath Test and So You’ve Been Publicly Shamed comes  The Castle, a darkly comic trip to the furthest reaches of the masculinity crisis. His only child is lured to a mysterious castle in the forests of New England late one night, sending Jon Ronson on an extraordinary adventure into a dark world of unmoored men desperately searching for purpose and control. What exactly is “Princessing”? Why did a lawn care influencer dress as a baby in front of billions of online viewers? And, more pressingly, why are two recently released murderers on their way to pay Jon a visit? Find out at Jon’s one-man show drawing on his trademark brand of humor, psychological insight, and unrivaled prescience. Doors at 7:00pm.

events.title: for colored girls who considered suicide / when the rainbow is enuf 50th Anniversary (SOLD OUT)
events.blurb:
FREE, $10-$15 suggested donation
 
This year marks the 50th anniversary of the Broadway debut of Ntozake Shange’s famed choropoem for colored girls who considered suicide / when the rainbow is enuf. First performed at the women’s bar Bacchanal right here in Albany before becoming the second play by a Black woman to run on Broadway,  for colored girls is a series of poetic monologues accompanied by dance movements and music. To honor Shange’s legacy, join amalee b., Briana Grogan, Jaine, Mukethe Kawinzi, Erica Lewis, Carl Nickolas, and Wendy M. Thompson. Curated by London Pinkney as they weave the work together. Doors at 5:30pm.

events.title: Helene Wecker: The Gates of Midnight
events.blurb:
FREE

Co-presented with JCC East Bay

Join us for an evening with Helene Wecker, author of the bestselling The Golem and the Jinni trilogy, reading from long-awaited The Gates of Midnight.  Wecker will discuss the trilogy, the joys and challenges of writing historical fantasy, and what it feels like to finish a writing project twenty years in the making. Doors at 6:00pm.

events.title: Freedom: Essays with Zinzi Clemmons
Ukraïne: Recipes and Stories from Kyiv to the Black Sea
events.blurb:
FREE

Co-presented with Omnivore Books on Food

Experience the joy and resilience of Ukrainian cuisine in a visually rich, travelogue-style cookbook filled with 100 traditional and modern recipes highlighting the comforting dishes, distinctive flavors, and time-honored techniques that make this food so extraordinary. Ukrainian chef Anna Voloshyna traveled across the diverse regions of her homeland―from the mountains to coastline, cities to grasslands, forests to wine country―collecting recipes, stories, and friendships to answer the question: What is Ukrainian cuisine? Joining Voloshyna on this appetizing and fascinating journey is food writer Paolo Bicchieri.

events.title: Decentered Arts presents Poolside Poets
events.blurb:
$30
 
Immerse yourself in a dreamy night of poetry, music, and dance by the pool at the breathtaking historic venue founded by Ken Fulk. Dress to impress (disco theme!), and remember to wear your dancing shoes. Performances by poets Bridget Clancy, Shane King Zackery, Jaír Griffin, Denise Masiel, spinelli, James Morehead, Maya Anne , and Papi Grande, alongside an epic musician, dancers, fashion, community, and more! Hosted by Rhea Joseph & Liz Cahill. Doors at 6:30pm.

events.title: A 22nd-Century Conservation Ethos for California
events.blurb:
FREE, $10-$15 suggested donation

Sponsored by Heyday Books
Co-presented with KALW

California’s landscapes have long been shaped by deep relationships between people and place. But that relationship has changed dramatically over time, especially with the rise of European American settlement and the erasure of Traditional Ecological Knowledge. Panelists Obi Kaufmann, creator of the California Field Atlas series; Laura Cunningham, award-winning author of A State of Change; and earth scientist and professional mountain biker Dillon Osleger examine how modern society has grown increasingly estranged from the natural world. Together, they imagine a new conservation ethos—one rooted in restoration, resilience, and reciprocity—and ask what it would take for Californians to leave the state healthier, more biodiverse, and more ecologically whole at the end of the 21st century than at its beginning. Moderated by Leslie Carol Roberts. Doors at 6:30pm.

events.title: Sweet and Lowdown: Poets at the Bar
events.blurb:
$12 adv / $15 door
 
This celebration of poetry collates a half-dozen poets’ stylings, live on our darkest, dankest stage. Featuring multi-hyphenate award winners Nancy Miller Gomez, Prairie Moon Dalton, Ibe Liebenberg, Leigh Lucas, and Preeti Vangani for a lurid evening of ebullient verse. Hosted by Litquake Artistic Director Graham Todd. Doors at 6:30 PM.

events.title: Peter King: The Game
events.blurb:
Pay-what-you-can for guaranteed seat; $45 for guaranteed seat with discounted book; FREE to walk-ups (space depending)

Are you ready for some football? Kick off a weekend of big games—including Cal’s home matchup with Wake Forest and culminating with the 49ers on Monday Night Football—by joining fellow fans and scholars of the game for an afternoon with award-winning sports columnist Peter King. For 40+ years, King unpacked the NFL for countless readers and mentored dozens of sportswriters along the way. Now, in The Game, King combines an in-depth history of the league with his signature vivid storytelling, thorough reporting, and keen understanding of the sport. Troy Aikman points out, “Peter King has stories no one else can tell.” King will share many of them with us, in conversation with Carmen Policy, one of the architects of the Niners' glory days. Doors at 4:00pm.

events.title: Heaven Looks Like Us: Palestinian Poetry
events.blurb:
FREE, $10-$15 suggested donation
 
Part of Words Around the World
Sponsored by Center for the Art of Translation
 Poetry has always served as a mode of resistance in Palestinian culture. In defiance of dispossession and decades of military siege, of a nakba that never ended, of historical and cultural obfuscation, of unrelenting violence and thousands of martyred people, the “power to narrate,” as Edward Said wrote, remains a necessary tool for self-determination. As Palestinian history remains haunted by exile, violence, and grief, there’s more here that’s also true: queer and feminist perspectives, eco-poetry, meditations on love and time, and lineages of protest. These poems reclaim that power to narrate, bridging borders, languages, and generations to forge new conversations around resistance and liberation. Featuring Haymarket Books' Heaven Looks Like Us anthology contributors Zeina Hashem Beck, Janine Mogannam, Deema Shehabi, Jen Siraganian, Priscilla Wathington, and Omar Zahzah. Doors at 6:30pm.

events.title: Irregular Feedback: Writers on Music
events.blurb:
$12 adv / $15 door
 
"Music makes the people come together... yeah." That's right, Madonna. You said it. So astute. Join cultural critic, essayist, and curator Micheal Foulk (Queer Film Theory 101) for an evening of writers writing about music! Inspired by the perpetual beat inside us all and the iconic music criticism and archival work of writer Hanif Abdurraqib, Michael-Vincent D'Anella-Mercanti, Kai Gault, Joan Granite, Brittany Newell, and Kochina Rude read work written exclusively for tonight, a literary deep dive into our favorite albums, genres, and musical artists of the past 60 years. Doors at 6:30pm.

events.title: Generation Women: Wins & Losses
events.blurb:
$25 / $3 early bird discount until October 11th (code earlybird15)

Co-presented with Generation Women

We’re pleased to once again welcome Generation Women, a live multigenerational storytelling series. One woman or nonbinary performer in their 20s, 30s, 40s, 50s, 60s, and 70s+ will share an original true story on the theme of “Wins & Losses,” whether personal, professional, psychological, or completely enigmatic. Founded by author Georgia Clark in New York City in 2017, the mission of Generation Women is to amplify underheard voices and create space for intergenerational connection and community. Featuring S.C. Bandreddi, Alexandra Romanoff, Kate Schatz, Bora Reed, Dashka Slater, and Sandra Jackson-Opoku. Hosted by writer, editor, and curator Samantha Schoech. Doors at 7:30pm.

events.title: FilBookFest
events.blurb:
FREE

Part of Words Around the World

Co-presented with Friends of the San Francisco Public Library, the Filipino American Center at SFPL, PAWA, and the San Francisco Public Library

The Filipino American International Book Festival (FilBookFest) returns in October for its 8th iteration, continuing its legacy as the largest Filipino American literary festival in the United States. Held during Filipino American History Month, FilBookFest brings together an exciting array of writers, scholars, and creatives from across the globe, including the U.S., Canada, and the Philippines, to the iconic San Francisco Public Library. Keynote speakers for 2026 include Randy Ribay, author of Patron Saints of Nothing & Nest of Tongues; Dr. Robyn Rodriguez, author of Contemporary Asian American Activism: Building Movements for Liberation; and Professor M. Evelina Galang, author of When the Hibiscus Falls and recipient of the inaugural PAWA Lifetime Achievement Award. Other featured authors include Mia Alvar, Marivi Soliven, Mia Manansala (US); Yvette Tan, Jet Tagasa and Jaya Jacobo (Philippines); Candy Gourlay (UK), as well as children’s authors Tracy Badua (US) and Analene Go (Canada). The festival will also feature a bustling marketplace with tables from PAWA Books, Arkipelago Books, Eastwind Books, and Bel Canto Books. For a full program schedule and author lineup, visit filbookfestival.org.

events.title: Read the Room: Books Not Bans
events.blurb:
FREE, $10-$15 suggested donation
 
Books Not Bans together with City Lights and Litquake present a party for everyone who loves reading. Join us for an afternoon filled with connection, revelry, music, games and stories. Featuring performances, readings, and all kinds of stuff from Syr Hayati Beker, Shoshana von Blanckensee, Kevin Dublin, W.S. Gong, Hyazinth, Sean Owens, and Sumiko Saulson. Hosted by Books Not Bans founder Becka Robbins. Proceeds from this event support Books Not Bans.

events.title: ZYZZYVA Movie Matinee: Amarcord
Dorothy Lazard: Behind the Desk at the Main
events.blurb:
FREE, $10-$15 suggested donation

Co-presented with Museum of the African Diaspora

Dorothy Lazard’s celebrated 2023 memoir What You Don’t Know Will Make a Whole New World traced the beloved Oakland librarian’s coming of age through books. Now she’s back to tell more of her story, relating her experiences over two decades at the Oakland Public Library. Along the way, she makes a powerful case for the essential role of the public library as a pillar of democratic ideals, and she crafts a tribute to the library workers who have devoted their careers to supporting intellectual freedom as well as to the countless Oaklanders whom she had the privilege of serving. Lazard will be joined in conversation by Pendarvis Harshaw, community engagement reporter at KQED. Doors at 1:30pm.

events.title: Picturing the Past: Graphic Novelists on History and Memory
events.blurb:
FREE, $10-$15 suggested donation

Sponsored by Berkeleyside

Through memoir, history, fiction, or a combination, these four talented creators use cartoons to give readers a vivid glimpse into the past. Frederick Noland shares the epic story of Major Taylor, the “world’s fastest man,” a global cycling sensation despite the incessant racism the Black athlete encountered. In Armaveni, Nadine Takvorian draws on her own family history to relate the heartbreaking history of the Armenian genocide. Emil Wilson’s The Nightingales blends fact and fiction in a personal story of the 1980s AIDS crisis. And Maria van Lieshout’s graphic novel Song of a Blackbird pairs the stories of two Dutch teens, one contemporary and one bearing witness to Nazi atrocities. Brief visual presentations will be followed by a conversation led by graphic memoirist Briana Loewinsohn. Doors at 6:30pm.

events.title: Jean-Baptiste Phou: Coming Out of My Skin
events.blurb:
FREE, $10-$15 suggested donation

Part of Words Around the World
Sponsored by Center for the Art of Translation
Co-presented with Villa Albertine

Having grown up as a Cambodian immigrant in France, Jean-Baptiste Phou has long explored the challenges and contradictions of the Asian diaspora experience throughout his artistic career. However, up until now, he’s always been careful not to raise issues of sexuality—in particular, his homosexuality. In his recent memoir, Coming Out of My Skin, the artist shifts his focus to examining the role his ethnic origin has played in the construction of his sexual identity and his romantic relationships in a predominantly white environment. An astute observer of the various ways in which his body has been perceived, Phou asks: how does a marginalized person develop emotionally and build, reclaim, and express their sexuality? How does this inform the experience of a queer Asian person navigating predominantly white cultural spaces? In conversation with César Cadabes, Artistic Director for the GLBTQ Asian Pacific Alliance (GAPA) Theatre. Doors at 6:30pm

events.title: An Evening Spell: Trans Poetry & Hardware Hang
events.blurb:
FREE, $10-$15 suggested donation
 
An evening time experimental live hardware performance, reading, and party featuring trans hardware musicians and poets. Featured musicians Cat Laugian and Daria Lourd. Curated by Jaelynn Walls.

events.title: FilBookFest
events.blurb:
FREE

Part of Words Around the World

Co-presented with Friends of the San Francisco Public Library, the Filipino American Center at SFPL, PAWA, and the San Francisco Public Library

The Filipino American International Book Festival (FilBookFest) returns in October for its 8th iteration, continuing its legacy as the largest Filipino American literary festival in the United States. Held during Filipino American History Month, FilBookFest brings together an exciting array of writers, scholars, and creatives from across the globe, including the U.S., Canada, and the Philippines, to the iconic San Francisco Public Library. Keynote speakers for 2026 include Randy Ribay, author of Patron Saints of Nothing & Nest of Tongues; Dr. Robyn Rodriguez, author of Contemporary Asian American Activism: Building Movements for Liberation; and Professor M. Evelina Galang, author of When the Hibiscus Falls and recipient of the inaugural PAWA Lifetime Achievement Award. Other featured authors include Mia Alvar, Marivi Soliven, Mia Manansala (US); Yvette Tan, Jet Tagasa and Jaya Jacobo (Philippines); Candy Gourlay (UK), as well as children’s authors Tracy Badua (US) and Analene Go (Canada). The festival will also feature a bustling marketplace with tables from PAWA Books, Arkipelago Books, Eastwind Books, and Bel Canto Books. For a full program schedule and author lineup, visit filbookfestival.org.

events.title: How to Exi(s)t: A Poet’s Memoir with Truong Tran
events.blurb:
FREE
 
Co-presented with City Lights
 
How to Exi(s)t: A Poet’s Memoir is an experiment in nonlinear autobiography by the author of the American Book Award–winning Book of the Other, Truong Tran. Beginning in the present—at a writing residency in the aftermath of this success—How to Exi(s)t unpeels the layers between present and past in bursts of brief poetic essays. Unsparing, even caustic in its insistence on racism as a dominant note of American life, but marked by surprising tenderness and humor, How to Exi(s)t is a compelling portrayal of Tran’s pedagogical philosophy as well as an interrogation of a poetic language that conceals as much as it reveals. In conversation with Garrett Caples.

events.title: Listen to Your Elders: An Elder Project Reading
events.blurb:
FREE, $10-$15 suggested donation
 
Co-presented with San Francisco Public Library
 
Litquake’s Elder Project brings creative writing and storytelling workshops to retirement communities across San Francisco and Oakland. Seniors participate in reading, storytelling, discussion, hands-on creative writing, and in-class sharing sessions to explore their own stories, the stories of their communities, and stories about the world, while using the techniques of fiction, poetry, and creative nonfiction that they've learned in classes. Share in the beauty of their words, hear their stories, listen to your elders.

Watch the stream here.

events.title: Menopause Extravaganza: The Science and Culture of a Subject No One Used to Want to Talk About
events.blurb:
$10 advance / $15 door

Co-presented with Gray Area Theater

Menopause, a natural consequence of aging, has for centuries been alternately ignored and belittled, seen mostly through a male lens of bafflement, repugnance, and boilerplate misogyny. Now, however, a growing body of women and their doctors are rejecting this traditional view, developing new therapies and strategies as well as ways to appreciate the new freedoms it can offer. This energizing (and overdue) afternoon features Dr. Louann Brizendine, author of The Female Brain, reading from her forthcoming Your Brain on Menopause and joining other panelists in a conversation led by Keli Dailey: Dr. Sarah Isquick, a double board-certified OBGYN and concierge gynecologist specializing in hormonal health; psychiatrist Dr. Alecia Greenlee; and menopause doula Lasara Firefox Allen, author of Genderqueer Menopause. Select performers from The Menopause Monologues® will kick off the event.Bring your friends for a conversation-sparking afternoon. Doors at 2:30pm.

events.title: A Celebration of César Vallejo's Trilce
events.blurb:
FREE

Part of Words Around the World
 Sponsored by Center for the Art of Translation
 Co-presented with City Lights and New York Review of Books


 First published in 1922, and rich in startling neologisms and other forms of verbal play, Trilce is a blazingly vivid revelation of what poetry can be, at once a love poem, a poem of erotic urgency and frustration, a poem of family life, of political fury, a lament for the dead, a work of intense privacy and an address to the world. In this new edition of Trilce from NYRB—the recipient of the prestigious Premio Valle Inclán for the best translation from Spanish into English—the translators Helen Dimos and William Rowe accompany each poem with a gloss. Their incisive commentary on these legendarily challenging poems opens them up to new understanding while inviting readers to find their own pathways to and through them.

events.title: Woof: A Celebration of Our Canine Companions
events.blurb:
FREE, $10-$15 suggested donation

Co-presented with LitCamp and Page Street

San Francisco is famously home to more dogs than kids, so let's celebrate our love for all things canine with a reading of fifteen super-short pieces about our furry, tail-wagging friends. There will be dog treats from local suppliers, plus complimentary Prosecco, wine, and fancy nonalcoholic drinks. Note: Much as we would love to see your canine companion, due to the (very) crowded nature of these events, we have to regretfully request they remain at home. The event will be emceed by LitCamp founder Janis Cooke Newman. Doors at 6:30pm.

events.title: Living in the Shadow of Silicon Valley
events.blurb:
FREE, $10–$15 suggested donation

Sponsored by Mission Local
Co-presented with Bay Area Book Festival and San Francisco Public Library

Sure, Silicon Valley’s wealth, power, and technological innovation loom large over the entire Bay Area—but what about the rest of us? Tonight we’ll hear from three authors who can share deep knowledge of Silicon Valley’s effects on Bay Area housing, economic inequality, urban planning, and public policy. Investigative journalist Brian Barth (Front Street: Resistance and Rebirth in the Tent Cities of Techlandia), anthropologist Manissa Maharawal (Anti-Eviction: The Fight Against Tech-Led Gentrification in San Francisco), and journalist Jonathan Weber (City on the Edge: Technology, Politics, and the Fight for the Soul of San Francisco) will be joined by architect and urban planner Vinita Goyal. Doors at 5:30pm.

events.title: Alain Damasio: Horde of the Counterwind
events.blurb:
FREE, $10–$15 suggested donation

Part of Words Around the World
Sponsored by Center for the Art of Translation
Co-presented with Villa Albertine

In 2004, Alain Damasio’s Horde of the Counterwind: An Epic Voyage to the Upper Reaches gained acclaim as France’s genre-defining sci-fi odyssey of the 21st century, inspiring the celebrated video game Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 and igniting the imaginations of millions around the world. Now, this seminal work appears in English translation for the very first time, offering even more readers the opportunity to experience a masterpiece of epic scope and visionary world-building in which twenty-three adventurers climb endlessly against the wind that plagues their desolate homeland. Their only purpose: identifying the mysterious source where eight centuries of past climbers have tried and failed. Join Damasio and Horde’s English translator, Alexander Dickow, for a conversation moderated by award-winning writer and translator Edward Gauvin. Doors at 6:30pm.

events.title: Pitchapalooza
events.blurb:
Pay what you can ($15 suggested) for guaranteed seat; FREE to walk-ups (space depending)

Pitchapalooza is American Idol for books (only kinder and gentler). Twenty writers, selected at random, will pitch their book for one minute only! Judges (including The Book Doctors, Arielle Eckstut and David Henry Sterry) will help you improve your pitch, not tell you how bad it is. Judges critique everything from idea to style to marketplace potential, and authors gain concrete advice as well as a greater understanding of the publishing industry. Whether potential authors pitch themselves, or simply listen to the critiques, Pitchapalooza is educational and entertaining for one and all. At evening’s end, the judges will pick a winner. Like the dozens of Pitchapalooza winners who have gone from talented amateurs to professionally published authors, this lucky participant will receive an introduction to an agent or publisher. Doors at 6:30pm.

events.title: Memoirs: Writing Against Silence or Erasure
events.blurb:
FREE, $10–$15 suggested donation

Co-presented with Memoir Nation

These four memoirists are, in different ways, writing into spaces where their experience has been minimized, misread, or actively suppressed. Judy Juanita's California Fever Dream spans sixty years of writing focused on Black activism and feminism. In I Love You So Many, journalist Terria Smith shares lessons learned from a career sharing stories about the richness of Native people’s lives. Elena Dudum's They Told Me Back Home Would Be Beautiful is a call to action against institutional silencing and censorship. Finally, Caroline Paul has spent her career writing women into adventure narratives that historically excluded them, most recently in Why Fly. Brooke Warner and Grant Faulkner, co-founders of the Memoir Nation podcast and online community, will guide a compelling discussion on the power of this truth-telling form. Doors at 6:30pm.

events.title: Brian Evenson: Phantom Limb
Celebrating 50 Years of Publishers Group West
events.blurb:
FREE, $10–15 suggested donation

Sponsored by Publishers Group West

From a shoestring investment of $500 in 1976, Berkeley-based Publishers Group West grew, by the turn of the century, into the US’s largest distributor of independent presses. Since then, it’s maintained its focus on resilience, innovation, and a passion for independent publishing—not to mention the value of throwing a really great party. We’ll toast to a half-century of PGW, which continues to distribute books for 150 publisher clients, including some beloved local presses. How does PGW’s history reflect the larger story of Bay Area publishing? And how can lessons learned over the past fifty years inform its future? Join PGW founder Charlie Winton, executive VP Sean Shoemaker, VP of field sales Elise Cannon, and Litquake co-founder Jack Boulware for a walk down memory lane—and stick around to buy a beverage or two from Clio’s on-site bar. Doors at 6:30pm.

events.title: Rapture: the art that moves us
events.blurb:
FREE, $10-$15 suggested donation
 
An interactive evening of poetry, music, drumming, and call-and-response performance where audiences are invited to clap, sing, sway, and become part of the rhythm. Rapture transforms the reading into a collective, full-body experience of sound, movement, and shared energy. Featuring poets and performers BB Brown, Trinh Lê, Sun Park, Matt Pacelli, Kimi Sugioka, and Joe Wadlington. Curated by London Pinkney. Doors at 5:30pm.

events.title: Nafissa Thompson-Spires: The Four Wives and Five Deaths of Richard Milford
Kearny Street Workshop presents APAture Literary Showcase
events.blurb:
$15

 APAture, the only festival to put the focus on emerging Asian Pacific American artists, returns from Oct. 17th to Dec. 12th for its 27th year. This year's theme, GENERATION, turns our focus toward what we inherit, what we cultivate, and what we pass on—seeding growth for the future health of our communities while honoring the artistic lineages that have brought us to this moment. As we consider what the next generation of artists will hold and shape, we celebrate creative inheritance as an active, collective practice, one that bridges past, present, and future through art. What do you carry forward, and what will you leave behind? This year's literary showcase features writers Alyson Sagala, Bianca Datta, Brandon Vu, Leslie Nguyen-Okwu, Mai-Linh Hong, May-Li Khoe, Monica Korde, Neha M. Sampat, Rose Wong, and Vina Vo. Doors at 6:00pm.

events.title: Artificial Intimacy: Sherry Turkle and A.I.
events.blurb:
Co-presented with Yerba Buena Center for the Arts

Sherry Turkle has spent decades studying how digital technologies isolate us from one another. Now, in her latest book, Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk To Machines, the psychologist who pioneered our understanding of human-computer relationships explores the seductive and beguiling nature of chatbots presented as “perfect” companions. How does their popularity point to existing wells of deep loneliness in our current culture, and how does increasing reliance on a one-sided digital ear affect users’ ability to maintain offscreen relationships with other humans? In conversation with New Yorker cartoonist Amy Kurzweil, whose graphic novel Artificial: A Love Story suggests an alternate path in which A.I. isn’t used as a human connection substitute, but rather a tool to support and deepen the real-world relationships we already have. The conversation is part of Free Wednesdays at YBCA, which offers extended gallery hours, hands-on afternoon art-making, and special evening programs—all for free. Doors at 6:00pm.

events.title: California Journeys
events.blurb:
FREE, $10–15 suggested donation

Co-presented with KALW

Taking the driver’s seat on tonight’s narrative journey through California is Grant Faulkner, whose recent “flash novel” something out there in the distance pairs short, perfectly crystallized prose vignettes with Gail Butensky’s photographs of the American West. Riding shotgun is Irena Smith, whose memoir Troika is a modern-day Odyssey set in California’s Central Coast, as three generations of women share profound family stories and create new ones. As for Angelica Glass, she’ll opt out of driving altogether—her memoir Scavenging Beauty relates her quest to find healing while traversing all the streets in Santa Cruz County by foot. In true travelogue style, their conversation will be accompanied by photos illustrating each author’s journey. Doors at 6:30pm.

events.title: Vigdis Hjorth: Repetition
All Hallows Eve: An Evening with Ellen Datlow & Friends
Fire, Earth, Air & Water: Nik Sharma on the Science of Better Cooking
events.blurb:
$30 Book Society Members / $45 General Public

Sponsored by Chronicle Books
Media sponsorship by Berkeleyside
Co-presented with Book Society

With books like Season and The Flavor Equation, award-winning cookbook author and America's Test Kitchen Editor in Residence Nik Sharma has earned a reputation for blending storytelling and science with recipes that are seasonal, reliable, and delicious. In his fourth cookbook, Fundamentals of Flavor: 100 Recipes for the Science of Better Cooking, this former molecular biologist shows home cooks how four elements—fire, earth, air, and water—shape the way we cook and taste. In conversation with food writer Soleil Ho, Sharma will lead an interactive evening in the spirit of a test kitchen: an intimate conversation with tastings of recipes from the book. Doors at 6:00pm. Ticket includes tastings and wine or a non-alcoholic beverage. $10 of each ticket supports Litquake.

events.title: Her Story, History, Their Story, Whose Story? Facts and Fictions in Historical Queer Books
events.blurb:
$10 / FREE for GLBT Historical Society Members

Co-presented with Bay Area Reporter and GLBT Historical Society

What are the rules of engagement when telling historical tales about the lives of LGBTQ characters? Authors and scholars compare notes on their fictional and nonfiction works that resonate realistically, and even those that are completely fantastical yet set in the real world’s past. Featuring authors Mark Abramson, Lucy Jane Bledsoe, Joey Cain, and Katie Gilmartin. Moderated by Bay Area Reporter arts editor and author Jim Provenzano. Doors at 5:30pm.

events.title: California's Diverse Food and Farming Movements
events.blurb:
FREE

Co-presented with Book Club of California

Californians tend to think and talk a lot about food—not just who has the best farmers’ markets or where to find the latest Instagram-famous pastry, but also about how the ways we grow, harvest, distribute, and consume food can best serve goals related to climate, social justice, and collective well-being. In his new book, North Stars of Emancipation: California’s Diverse Food and Farming Movements, researcher and activist Antonio Roman-Alcalá finds guidance on all these questions in our state’s grassroots food movements, and in the vision of Black, Indigenous, Latinx, and other people who are leading the way. Joining Roman-Alcalá in conversation is one of those leaders, Sara Calvosa Olson, author of Chími Nu’am: Native Californian Foodways for the Contemporary Kitchen. Member/guest reception at 5:30pm.

events.title: Vigdis Hjorth: Repetition (Marin Edition)
Ben Ehrenreich: Hold Still
events.blurb:
FREE

 Co-presented with City Lights
 

 In the months after his mother Barbara’s death, author and essayist Ben Ehrenreich set himself the task of writing a story every day. Leaving open the question of what a “story” might be, some entries ended up fable-like tales involving animals doing surprising things. Others were closer to journal entries, many of them about his daughter, who was nearly three at the time, and who was trying to understand death herself at the same time that she was voraciously exploring the living world. This deeply moving collection of those daily journeys into storytelling—a finely crafted combination of fiction, memoir, and poetic prose—is both profound and satisfyingly whimsical. In conversation with Daniel Gumbiner.

events.title: Lights, Camera, Action: Porchlight Storytelling on the Big Screen
events.blurb:
$20 adv / $25 door
 

 The Bay Area’s long-running Porchlight storytelling series returns to Litquake for this special cinematic edition, featuring tales of the silver screen from the Bay’s finest writers and comedians including Jack Boulware, Mukethe Kawinzi, Ali Liebegott, Pia Hinckle, TK Moyer, and sam sax. Co-hosted by Arline Klatte and Beth Lisick. Music by Marc Capelle. Doors at 7:00pm.

events.title: Hieu Minh Nguyen & Friends
Chad Harbach: The Brightness
events.blurb:
$15 / $3 early bird discount until October 18th (code: earlybird16)
$35 for presale signed book (ticket not included)
 
From the bestselling author of literary sensation The Art of Fielding comes an urgent, deeply felt story of friendship, art, love, and grief, following two young women on the brink of irrevocable change. Parties and weddings, messy hookups and marred friendships, art and love and grief—The Brightness follows the electric, chaotic, everything-can-happen lives of Pella and her best friend, Irma, as they fumble their way out of sleepy, Midwestern Westish College and into a larger world that will upend their connection and everything they thought they understood about their own place within it. In stunning scenes and spectacular characters—each drawn with an almost superhuman vividness and humanity—Chad Harbach captures that specific, shimmering anxiety of your twenties when life still feels wide open, even as hard and irreversible choices start closing in. In conversation with novelist Eirinie Carson. Doors at 7:30pm.

Order a signed copy of The Brightness here (note: does not include general admission ticket).

events.title: Five Tastes: Delicious Recipes for Chinese Flavors with Fuchsia Dunlop
events.blurb:
FREE

Part of Words Around the World
Co-presented with Omnivore Books on Food

Over thousands of years, Chinese chefs have mastered how to combine the five tastes―sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and pungent―harmoniously in a dish. In her latest cookbook, Five Tastes, Fuchsia Dunlop shares with home cooks 120 easy recipes inspired by culinary traditions across China. She includes both old-fashioned favorites and her freshly invented dishes that combine Chinese flavors with produce found in any Western market or supermarket. Join us at Omnivore Books to meet this superstar of Chinese cuisine and learn about her processes for recipe research and development. In conversation with Harold McGee.

events.title: Walter Mosley: Hanging and Burning
Carolina Pihelgas: The Cut Line
events.blurb:
FREE, $10–15 suggested donation

Part of Words Around the World
Sponsored by Center for the Art of Translation

Poet, author, translator, and editor Carolina Pihelgas is a leading literary figure in her home country of Estonia. Now, with The Cut Line, translated by Darcy Hurford, Pihelgas’s “extraordinary” (Estonian Literary Magazine) prose writing is available to English readers for the first time. In fewer than 100 pages, Pihelgas takes readers to a near-future Estonian countryside, plagued by the effects of climate change and poised for an impending conflict. These hints of future violence recall the protagonist’s own troubled history, even as she attempts to find serenity and order in the rhythms of nature and simple work. Joining Pihelgas in conversation is Sasha Vasilyuk, award-winning author of the novel Your Presence Is Mandatory. Doors at 6:30pm.

events.title: Lift Every Voice: A Festival Finale in Verse
events.blurb:
FREE, $10-15 suggested donation
 
Coming to us from Chicago, Phillip B. Williams brings us his newest collection Lift Every Voice, a staggering tribute to personal and collective evolutions, a vital chorus that answers only to God, community, and the empowered self. What better way to ground us on the penultimate night of Litquake 2026? Litquake invites you in alongside poets Fatimah Asghar, Stephanie Horvath, D.A. Powell, D.M. Spratley, and Phillip B. Williams to bear witness to the beauty and resiliency of our words and community.. Hosted by Litquake’s Artistic Director Graham Todd. Doors at 6:30pm.

events.title: Queerly Beloved: A Celebration of LGBTQ+ Writing in Foglifter
events.blurb:
FREE, $10-15 suggested donation
 
Co-presented with Foglifter and The Stud
 
Foglifter—created by and for LGBTQ+ writers and readers—continues the San Francisco Bay Area’s tradition of groundbreaking queer and trans writing, with an emphasis on publishing those multi-marginalized (BIPOC, youth, elders, and people with disabilities). Queerly Beloved is a celebration of the latest queer writing coming out in Foglifter's newest journals, online exclusives, and Start a Riot! Chapbook series. Limited print copies of the newest issue will be available for purchase—get them before anyone else! Featuring: Brent Armendinger, Juda Ātman, KB Brookins, Reggie Edmonds-Vásquez, Alix Perry, and Allegra Wilson! ASL interpretation provided. Livestreamed at youtube.com/@foglifterpress/streams. Hosted by Baruch Porras Hernandez. Doors at 6:00pm.

events.title: Playlist Storytellers

Everyone has a song that found them at the right time. Welcome to Playlist Storytellers, a live event where a curated group of writers share personal stories about a song that found them just when they needed it. Featuring stories from authors Laleh Khadivi, Tomas Moniz, Courtney Desiree Morris, and Preeti Vangani. Doors at 7:30pm.
